level1.text: A cart of mass $1.5\,\text{kg}$ is on a frictionless table. A string tied to it pulls it horizontally with a force of $3.0\,\text{N}$. Draw the free-body diagram of the cart. What is the acceleration of the cart?

A mass of $0.60\,\text{kg}$ hangs from a string and descends with an acceleration of $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$. Air resistance is neglected. Draw the free-body diagram of the mass. What is the tension in the string?

A cart of mass $1.0\,\text{kg}$ is on a frictionless table. A light, inextensible string tied to it passes over a light, frictionless pulley at the edge of the table, and a mass of $0.40\,\text{kg}$ hangs from the end of the string. Air resistance is neglected.

Draw the free-body diagram of each body. What is the tension in the string when the bodies are moving?

Two identical bodies, each of mass $3.0\,\text{kg}$, hang at the ends of a light string over a light, frictionless pulley. The bodies are at rest. Draw the free-body diagram of one body. What is the tension in the string?

Two carts of masses $1.0\,\text{kg}$ and $2.0\,\text{kg}$ are tied together with a light string on a frictionless track, and air resistance is neglected. A horizontal pulling force of $12\,\text{N}$ acts on the lighter cart, and the carts move together. What is the common acceleration of the carts?

A cart is on a frictionless table and is tied by a string over a pulley to a hanging mass. The mass descends and the cart accelerates. The string and the pulley are light, and air resistance is neglected. How are the tension $T$ in the string and the weight $G_2$ of the hanging mass related?
level1.answer: $T$ is smaller than $G_2$, because the net force on the hanging mass points downward

choices.text: $T$ is equal to $G_2$, because the string supports the hanging mass with its full weight
choices.feedback: That would be true only if the mass were at rest or moving at a constant speed. Now the mass accelerates downward, so its net force is not zero and $T$ is smaller than the weight.

choices.text: $T$ is greater than $G_2$, because the string also pulls the cart forward
choices.feedback: The string pulls the hanging mass upward and the cart forward with the same force $T$, but this does not add any force. If $T$ were greater than the weight, the net force on the hanging mass would point up and the mass would not descend.

choices.text: $T$ is half of $G_2$, because the string shares its force between two bodies
choices.feedback: The string does not share its force between the bodies: it pulls each body with the same force $T$. The relation to the weight depends on the masses, not on a fixed half.

choices.text: $T$ is smaller than $G_2$, because the net force on the hanging mass points downward
choices.feedback: Correct: the mass accelerates downward, so by Newton's second law $G_2 - T = m_2 a$ and the net force points down. Therefore $T < G_2$.

level1.text: Two bodies of masses $0.30\,\text{kg}$ and $0.70\,\text{kg}$ hang at the ends of a light, inextensible string over a pulley. The pulley is light and frictionless, and air resistance is neglected. The bodies are released. Draw the free-body diagram of each body. What is the common acceleration of the bodies?

A cart is on a frictionless table and is tied by a string over a pulley to a descending hanging mass. You are drawing the free-body diagram of the cart. Which forces act on the cart along the table? Which statement is correct?
level1.answer: Only the tension in the string, because the weight of the hanging mass acts on the hanging mass and not on the cart

choices.text: The tension in the string and the weight of the hanging mass, because the hanging mass also pulls the cart through the string
choices.feedback: The weight of the hanging mass is the force of the Earth on the hanging mass, not on the cart. The string transmits the tension $T$ to the cart, and that is already the whole effect of the string. Drawing the weight in the free-body diagram of the cart would add a force that does not act on the cart.

choices.text: Only the tension in the string, because the weight of the hanging mass acts on the hanging mass and not on the cart
choices.feedback: Correct: the free-body diagram of the cart includes only the forces acting on the cart. The weight acts on the hanging mass, and the string transmits the effect to the cart as the tension $T$, which is the only horizontal force on the cart.

choices.text: Only the weight of the hanging mass, because it sets the cart moving and the string merely transmits it to the cart
choices.feedback: The string does not transmit the weight as such. If the string pulled the cart with the whole weight $m_2 g$, the net force on the hanging mass would be zero and the mass would not descend. The force $T$ of the string is smaller than the weight.

choices.text: The tension in the string and the force of kinetic energy, because the cart moves forward on the table
choices.feedback: Motion does not bring any force of its own: kinetic energy is energy, not a force. The free-body diagram includes only forces that arise from interactions, such as the tension.

level2.text:
A crane's rope lifts a crate of mass $50\,\text{kg}$. Below it, a second crate of mass $30\,\text{kg}$ hangs from another rope. The crates accelerate upward with an acceleration of $1.2\,\text{m/s}^2$.

The ropes are light and inextensible, and air resistance is neglected.

Draw the free-body diagram of each crate in your notebook before you open the solution. What is the tension in the crane's rope?

Bodies of masses $0.50\,\text{kg}$ and $1.0\,\text{kg}$ hang at the ends of a light, inextensible string over a pulley. The pulley is light and frictionless, and air resistance is neglected. The bodies are released. Draw the free-body diagram of each body. What is the tension in the string?

Two sleds of masses $3.0\,\text{kg}$ and $2.0\,\text{kg}$ are on ice. The sleds are tied together with a light rope. The heavier sled is pulled horizontally with a force of $20\,\text{N}$ by another rope, and the sleds move together. Friction and air resistance are neglected. Draw the free-body diagram of each sled. What is the tension in the rope between the sleds?

Two bodies hang at the ends of a light, inextensible string over a pulley. The mass of the lighter one is $0.60\,\text{kg}$. The bodies are released, and the heavier one descends with an acceleration of $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$. The pulley is light and frictionless, and air resistance is neglected. Draw the free-body diagram of each body. What is the mass of the heavier body?

In an Atwood machine, two masses hang at the ends of a light, inextensible string over a pulley, and their total mass is always $M = 0.500\,\text{kg}$. The pulley is light and frictionless. The mass difference $\Delta m = m_2 - m_1$ is changed by moving small masses from one mass to the other, and for each mass difference the acceleration $a$ of the heavier mass is measured. The table shows example data of the measurements.

a) From the equations of motion of the two masses, derive a formula for calculating $a$ from the mass difference $\Delta m$.

b) Draw the $(\Delta m, a)$ graph and fit a straight line through the origin to it. Determine the acceleration of free fall $g$ from the slope of the line.

The answer box takes the acceleration of free fall from part b).

data.caption: Acceleration of an Atwood machine at different mass differences (example data)

level2.text:
A cart of mass $1.20\,\text{kg}$ is on a frictionless track and is tied by a light, inextensible string over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging mass. The cart is released from rest with different hanging masses, and the acceleration $a$ of the cart is measured each time. The table shows example data of the measurements.

From the measurement in which the hanging mass is $0.50\,\text{kg}$, determine the tension in the string using the equation of motion of the cart. Check the result with the equation of motion of the hanging mass from the same measurement. First draw the free-body diagram of each body.

The answer box takes the tension obtained from the equation of motion of the cart.

data.caption: Acceleration of the cart with different hanging masses (example data)

level2.text:
A cart of mass $2.0\,\text{kg}$ is on a frictionless table. A light, inextensible string tied to it passes over a light, frictionless pulley, and a mass of $0.50\,\text{kg}$ hangs from the end of the string. The bodies are released, and air resistance is neglected.

A student's solution: “Only the string acts on the cart in the horizontal direction, so $T = m_1 a$. For the hanging mass, $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$. I substituted the first into the second: $m_2 g - m_1 a = m_2 a$. From this I solved $a = \dfrac{m_2 g}{m_1} = 2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$.”

Find the error in the student's solution and calculate the correct acceleration. Also draw the free-body diagram of each body.

The answer box takes the correct acceleration.

On a frictionless table there is a trolley of mass $1.6\,\text{kg}$. A light, inextensible string tied to it passes over a light, frictionless pulley at the edge of the table, and a weight of mass $0.40\,\text{kg}$ hangs from the end of the string. The objects are released from rest, and air resistance is neglected.

Then the experiment is done the other way round: on the table there is a $0.40\,\text{kg}$ trolley and from the end of the string hangs a $1.6\,\text{kg}$ weight. How does the tension $T$ in the string change when the second experiment is compared with the first?

choices.text: The tension becomes four times as large.
choices.feedback: Here the tension has been assumed to depend on the weight of the hanging mass, which becomes four times as large. When the objects accelerate, the net force on the weight points down, so $T$ is smaller than the weight of the weight.

Correct: when the tension is calculated from the equations of motion in both experiments, the result is the same, $T \approx 3.1\,\text{N}$. Next choose the reason that explains why swapping the masses does not change it.

Here the acceleration has been assumed to be the same, because the total mass does not change, and $T = m_1 a$ has been reduced along with the mass of the trolley. The acceleration, however, becomes four times as large, because the weight of the hanging mass becomes four times as large.

reasons.text: The string supports the hanging weight, so the tension is the weight of the weight, $T = m_2 g$.
reasons.feedback: This is a common misconception in the chapter. Only at rest is $T = m_2 g$. When the weight goes down accelerating, $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$ is positive, so $T < m_2 g$ in both experiments.

reasons.text: The total mass does not change, so the acceleration does not change, and $T = m_1 a$ follows the mass of the trolley.
reasons.feedback: The total mass is the same, but the system is accelerated by the weight $m_2 g$ of the hanging mass, and it becomes four times as large. So $a$ becomes four times as large while $m_1$ becomes a quarter.

reasons.text: In the formula $T = \tfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g$ the product and the sum of the masses stay the same when they are swapped.
reasons.feedback: Correct: the product $m_1 m_2 = 0.64\,\text{kg}^2$ and the sum $m_1 + m_2 = 2.0\,\text{kg}$ are the same in both experiments.

reasons.text: The string is inextensible, so the trolley and the weight have the same magnitude of acceleration $a$.
reasons.feedback: The statement is true, but it does not explain the answer. The same acceleration holds in both experiments, and it does not tell how $T$ changes when the masses are swapped.

level3.text:
An elevator cabin of mass $800\,\text{kg}$ hangs from the end of a light, inextensible rope. The rope passes over a light, frictionless wheel, and at its other end is a counterweight of mass $1200\,\text{kg}$.

The counterweight descends and the cabin rises. Friction and air resistance are neglected.

Draw the free-body diagrams of the cabin and the counterweight. What is the force that the rope exerts on the axle of the wheel, when the wheel is light and the axle holds it in place?

A cart of mass $1.0\,\text{kg}$ is on a frictionless table and is tied by a light, inextensible string over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging mass.

The string breaks if its tension exceeds $3.0\,\text{N}$.

What is the greatest mass of the hanging mass for which the string still holds while the bodies are moving? First draw the free-body diagram of each body. Answer in kilograms.

A cart of mass $1.5\,\text{kg}$ is on a frictionless table and is tied by a light, inextensible string over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging mass of $0.50\,\text{kg}$. The cart is released from rest. How long does it take for the cart to travel $0.90\,\text{m}$? First draw the free-body diagram of each body.

A locomotive pulls three cars in a row on a straight horizontal track. The masses of the cars are $m_1 = 24\,\text{t}$, $m_2 = 18\,\text{t}$ and $m_3 = 12\,\text{t}$, and they are connected to each other by couplings. The mass of the locomotive is not counted, and the locomotive pulls the first car with the same force in both orders. Resistive forces are neglected, and the couplings are light and inextensible. The speed of the train is measured after the start. The table shows example data.

a) Determine the acceleration of the train from the table. Justify why it can be considered constant.

b) Draw the free-body diagram of each car and calculate the force of the coupling between cars 1 and 2.

c) The cars are rearranged so that the heaviest car is last and the lightest first, and the acceleration is the same. What is now the force of the coupling between the first and second cars? Does a coupling with a greatest permitted force of $20\,\text{kN}$ hold? Justify why the force of the coupling changed.

The answer box takes the force of the coupling from part b) in kilonewtons.

data.caption: Speed of the train after the start (example data)

level3.text:
A cart on a frictionless track has an unknown mass $m_1$. A light, inextensible string tied to it passes over a light, frictionless pulley, and a mass $m_2$ that varies hangs from the end of the string. The cart is released from rest, and the time $t$ that the hanging mass takes to descend $0.80\,\text{m}$ to the floor is measured. The table shows example data of the measurements.

a) Calculate the acceleration of the hanging mass from each measurement. From the equations of motion of the two bodies, derive a formula for calculating the mass of the cart from the mass $m_2$ and the acceleration $a$.

b) Determine the mass of the cart from each measurement and calculate their mean.

c) The hanging mass of $0.200\,\text{kg}$ hits the floor; the track is long enough, so the cart does not hit the pulley. What happens to the cart after that? Justify and calculate the speed of the cart at that moment.

The answer box takes the mean mass of the cart from part b).

data.caption: Descent time of the hanging mass over a distance of $0.80\,\text{m}$ (example data)
